followUps: 7:156 itself says 'My punishment - I afflict with it whom I will'. How does mercy that 'encompasses all things' fit with punishment?
What does iḥsān mean in everyday life? What would I actually do differently?
Why is so much Muslim preaching harsh if 3:159 forbids it?
doubter.why: The verses and hadith are real and well cited, but the page is a short collection of quotes with no explanation or practical guidance, and it skips the tension that its own verse (7:156) raises.

followUps: What do the Arabic words for mercy (raḥma, al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm) mean, and how central are they to Islam?
What is the story of the woman and the thirsty dog?
How does mercy in Islam compare with grace or compassion in other traditions?
outsider.why: The definition of iḥsān ('doing things beautifully and well') is clear, but the dog hadith is only a reference ('The woman who gave water to a thirsty dog (Bukhārī 3467)') with the story left out, and the hundred-parts hadith is said twice.

followUps: Where is the Jibrīl hadith defining iḥsān ('worship God as if you see Him', Muslim 8), and how does it relate to iḥsān 'in all things' (Muslim 1955)?
What did the scholars say about the conditional part of 7:156 ('I will decree it [especially] for those who fear Me')?
Which other hadith teach mercy to people and animals (e.g. 'the merciful are shown mercy'), with collection and grading?
student.why: The four hadith references are precise, but there is no tafsir, no scholar, and not even the best-known definition of iḥsān.

followUps: Is there research on practising compassion or kindness (wellbeing, behaviour) that relates to this ideal?
What does 'mercy in one hundred parts' mean? Is it read literally or as a figure of speech?
What concrete practices does the tradition prescribe for building mercy?
scientist.why: It is short and readable, but there is nothing to grasp beyond the quotes: no mechanism, no practice, no way to see what living this looks like.

followUps: I feel I have sinned too much for mercy. What does the tradition say to someone like me?
The woman who watered the dog: wasn't she forgiven despite her past? Please tell the whole story.
How do I show mercy to someone who hurt me without excusing the harm?
hurting.why: The message itself is comforting ('My mercy encompasses all things', ninety-nine parts kept for the Hereafter), but the most hopeful story, a sinner forgiven for watering a dog, is cut down to a citation.

followUps: The intro quotes only the mercy half of 7:156. Why leave out 'My punishment - I afflict with it whom I will' and the conditions that follow?
How does 'mercy to the worlds' fit with the Prophet's wars and the harsh punishments in Islamic law?
'Harsh preaching contradicts 3:159' is one line. Where is the honest look at the gap between this ideal and Muslim practice?
skeptic.why: It is one-sided: the opening summarises 7:156 as pure mercy, leaving out the punishment and conditions in the same verse, and 'the gap between ideal and practice' gets one sentence.

missing: An explanation of what mercy and iḥsān mean (raḥma and its root, al-Raḥmān/al-Raḥīm, the Jibrīl hadith on iḥsān) and what they look like in daily life
Honest treatment of the tension between mercy and punishment, starting with 7:156 itself
The dog hadith told as a story, including that the woman was a sinner who was forgiven
Practical guidance and examples of iḥsān toward people, animals and work
A real 'gap between ideal and practice' section, plus tafsir or named scholars
strengths: Verses quoted in full with Arabic, transliteration and attribution
3:159 used well to point out that harsh preaching goes against the Quran
